paragraphs: Swamiji often admired the Buddha's practical spirit. Buddha taught that everyone, whatever their caste, race or sect, has an equal right to God, to religion and to freedom. On most other questions he kept things simple: be practical.

One day five young Brahmins came to him in the middle of a heated argument. Each claimed that what his own people taught was the only road to truth, and they wanted Buddha to settle it. Buddha turned to one of them. Had he himself seen God? No. His father? No. His grandfather? No. His teachers? No again. Buddha put the same questions to the others, and every one of them had to admit that nobody they knew had ever seen God.

Then Buddha told them a story. In a certain village, a young man went around weeping and crying that he loved a woman so very much. The villagers asked who she was. He did not know. Where did she live? He did not know. What did she look like? He had no idea, but oh, how he loved her! Buddha asked the young Brahmins what they would call such a fellow. A fool, they said at once. Crying over a woman he had never seen and did not even know existed!
Buddha pointed out that they were doing exactly the same thing: fighting bitterly, almost ready to cut each other's throats, over a God whom neither they nor their ancestors had ever seen.

Humbled, they asked what they should do. Buddha asked whether their fathers had taught that God is angry or evil. No, they said, God is always pure. Then, said Buddha, if you become pure and good yourselves, won't you come much nearer to Him than by all this quarrelling? His whole advice fitted in one line: "Be pure and love everyone."
learn: It is easy to win arguments about big ideas we have never actually experienced. Buddha moves the question from 'who is right?' to 'how am I living?' Before you fight over beliefs online or in class, check whether you are living up to the goodness those beliefs describe.
